name: Key Practices (Shabbat, Festivals, Kosher)

objectives.text: Identify Shabbat as the weekly day of rest that Jewish families keep from Friday sunset to Saturday sunset
Name Passover and Hanukkah as Jewish celebrations and tell one thing each one remembers
Describe common Shabbat home practices such as lighting candles, blessing bread and wine, and sharing a family meal
Recall that Jewish dietary laws called kosher permit some foods and forbid others such as pork
Describe how Jewish families celebrate Hanukkah by lighting the menorah and Purim by reading the book of Esther
Identify the items on a Passover Seder plate and explain what each represents in the Exodus story
Summarize the main kosher rules including permitted animals, the separation of meat and dairy, and the draining of blood
Describe the High Holy Days of Rosh Hashanah and Yom Kippur and the practices of repentance and fasting connected with them
Explain Bar and Bat Mitzvah as the point at which a Jewish young person takes on responsibility for keeping the commandments
Describe the synagogue as a place of prayer, Torah reading, and community life and identify its main features
Compare the Jewish seventh-day Sabbath with the Christian Lord's Day in timing, purpose, and practice
Categorize the biblical pilgrimage festivals and the later festivals of Hanukkah and Purim by their origin and the events they remember
Analyze how the Levitical dietary laws marked Israel's separation from the nations as a holy people
Explain how practices such as Sabbath, circumcision, and dietary laws have preserved Jewish identity through exile and diaspora
Interpret the symbolism of the Passover Seder in light of Exodus 12 and Jesus' Last Supper as a Passover meal
Identify occasions in the Gospels when Jesus took part in Jewish festivals and explain what he taught at them
Explain the significance of the Western Wall and how Jewish practice shifted to prayer and synagogue worship after the destruction of the Temple
Compare how Orthodox, Conservative, and Reform Jewish communities differ in their observance of Shabbat and kashrut
Evaluate Sabbath-keeping for Christians using the Reformed teaching that the Sabbath continues as the Lord's Day on the first day of the week
Evaluate the difference between legalism and devotion in religious observance using Jesus' Sabbath teaching and the prophets' critique of empty ritual
Defend the Reformed position that Christians are free from the ceremonial law using the Jerusalem Council and related New Testament texts
Construct an account of how the Reformed tradition reads the Levitical feasts as types fulfilled in Christ's death, resurrection, and gift of the Spirit
Design a respectful approach to conversation with Jewish neighbors that represents their observances accurately and explains Christian convictions graciously

changes: Kept and reworded the real competencies (Shabbat, festivals, kosher, Seder, Bar/Bat Mitzvah, Sabbath vs Lord's Day, holiday categories, dietary separation, Seder symbolism, Jesus at the festivals, Western Wall, Christian Sabbath evaluation, legalism vs devotion, Acts 15 freedom, feasts fulfilled). Replaced the passive 'Observe a Seder plate' with identifying and explaining its items. Added missing practices: Shabbat home rituals, Hanukkah and Purim customs, High Holy Days, synagogue worship, practice as identity in diaspora, variation across Jewish movements, and respectful engagement. Narrowed whole-chapter citations to specific verses, added WCF 21.7-21.8, 20.1, WSC Q58-60 and Heidelberg Q103 where they state the doctrine, and kept WCF 7.5 and 19.3 for typology and ceremonial law.
